SafeAnchor: Preventing Cumulative Safety Erosion
in Continual Domain Adaptation of Large Language Models

Abstract.

Safety alignment in large language models is remarkably shallow: it is concentrated in the first few output tokens and reversible by fine-tuning on as few as 100 adversarial examples. This fragility becomes critical in real-world deployment, where models undergo sequential adaptation across domains such as medicine, law, and code, causing safety guardrails to erode cumulatively. Yet all existing safety-preserving methods target only single-task fine-tuning, leaving the multi-domain sequential setting entirely unaddressed.

We introduce SafeAnchor, a framework that anchors safety in place throughout continual adaptation. SafeAnchor first identifies low-rank safety subspaces in LoRA parameter space via Fisher Information eigendecomposition, then constrains domain-specific gradient updates to the orthogonal complement of these subspaces, and finally monitors for residual safety drift with threshold-triggered corrective replay. Evaluated on Llama-2-7B-Chat and Mistral-7B-Instruct across a three-domain pipeline and eight benchmarks, SafeAnchor retains 93.2% of original safety alignment, outperforming all baselines by 18–42 points, while matching unconstrained fine-tuning to within 1.5 points on domain tasks.

1. Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly adapted to specialized domains such as medicine, law, and code generation through continual fine-tuning on domain-specific data [34, 26]. In practice, a single model may undergo a sequence of adaptations as organizational needs evolve, forming a continual domain adaptation pipeline. While this sequential fine-tuning extends model capabilities, it poses a critical yet underexplored risk: the cumulative erosion of safety alignment.

Recent work has established that safety alignment in LLMs is surprisingly brittle. Qi et al. [31] demonstrated that current alignment primarily modifies the generative distribution over the first few output tokens, teaching models to begin with refusal phrases rather than embedding deep behavioral changes. Ji et al. [17] introduced alignment elasticity, showing that LLMs inherently resist alignment and revert to pre-training behavior upon further fine-tuning, with this effect intensifying at larger scales. Even benign fine-tuning on standard datasets can compromise safety guardrails [32], and as few as 100 adversarial examples can undo 100,000 safety training instances [40]. The “safety tax” documented by Huang et al. [13] further reveals a fundamental trade-off between safety and reasoning capability.

These findings reveal a fundamental vulnerability: each adaptation step risks degrading safety, and these degradations compound. Yet existing safety-preserving methods (Vaccine [14], RepNoise [33], Safe LoRA [9], SaLoRA [21], Lisa [11], SafeGrad [41]) all address only single-task adaptation. CL methods such as O-LoRA [39], InfLoRA [23], and GainLoRA [22] prevent task forgetting but ignore safety. Alssum et al. [1] and OGPSA [35] evaluate only single-task or the inverse problem. No existing work addresses safety during sequential multi-domain continual adaptation.

We propose SafeAnchor, a framework that anchors safety alignment in place while enabling effective continual domain adaptation of LLMs. SafeAnchor integrates three components whose combination addresses the sequential safety-preservation setting (Figure 1):

(1) Safety Subspace Identification (SSI) uses gradient-based Fisher Information analysis [2, 29, 44] to identify LoRA parameter directions encoding safety, updated incrementally after each domain via explicit subspace merging.

(2) Orthogonal Safety-Constrained Adaptation (OSCA) projects LoRA gradient updates onto the orthogonal complement of the safety subspace, extending gradient projection from single-task safety [41] and continual learning [23, 6] to the sequential safety-preservation setting.

(3) Cumulative Safety Monitoring (CSM) evaluates safety on a held-out probe set after each domain using LlamaGuard [15], triggering corrective replay when degradation exceeds a threshold.

We evaluate on Llama-2-7B-Chat [37] and Mistral-7B-Instruct [18] across eight benchmarks: domain (MedQA [19], LegalBench [7], HumanEval [3]), safety (HarmBench [28], TruthfulQA [24], BBQ [30], WildGuard [4]), and general (MMLU [8]). All results report mean ±\pm std over five seeds. SafeAnchor retains 93.2±1.093.2\pm 1.0% of original safety within 1.5 points of unconstrained fine-tuning, outperforming all baselines by 18–42 points.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    We identify and characterize the problem of safety-preserving continual domain adaptation, demonstrating that sequential fine-tuning causes compounding safety erosion unaddressed by existing methods.

  • •

    We propose SafeAnchor, integrating Fisher-based subspace identification, orthogonal gradient projection, and threshold-triggered monitoring into a unified framework for sequential safety preservation.

  • •

    We provide comprehensive experiments on two models and eight benchmarks with variance reporting, ablations, and sensitivity analysis, achieving state-of-the-art safety preservation.

2. Related Work

2.1. Fragility of Safety Alignment

Standard alignment techniques produce safety behaviors that are surprisingly shallow. Qi et al. [31] showed alignment concentrates in the first few output tokens; Ji et al. [17] demonstrated that LLMs exhibit alignment elasticity, reverting to pre-training behavior upon further fine-tuning, with this effect worsening at scale. Even benign fine-tuning compromises safety [32], and as few as 100 adversarial examples can undo extensive safety training [40]. The safety tax [13] further documents a fundamental safety–capability trade-off. Together, these findings motivate our work: if single-step fine-tuning already degrades safety, sequential multi-domain adaptation compounds the problem.

2.2. Safety-Preserving Fine-Tuning

Existing defenses operate at three stages [12]. Alignment-stage methods modify the base model before fine-tuning: Vaccine [14] produces perturbation-invariant embeddings, and RepNoise [33] removes harmful representations. Fine-tuning-stage methods constrain the adaptation process: Lisa [11] alternates alignment and task optimization, and SafeGrad [41] projects away safety-conflicting gradients. Post-fine-tuning methods adjust adapted weights: Safe LoRA [9] projects LoRA onto safety-aligned subspaces, and SaLoRA [21] orthogonalizes against safety features. Despite this rich landscape, every method addresses only single-task adaptation, leaving cumulative erosion across sequential domains unaddressed.

2.3. Continual Learning, Orthogonal Gradients, and Safety Subspaces

Continual learning for LLMs has converged on LoRA-based approaches [10, 34]. Orthogonal subspace methods are most relevant to our work: O-LoRA [39] learns each task in a subspace orthogonal to the column span of prior-task LoRA matrices, preventing inter-task interference but providing no mechanism for protecting a behavioral property; InfLoRA [23] pre-allocates per-task directions via SVD of input activations; OGD [6] provides the theoretical framing for gradient projection which we extend from task-preservation to safety-preservation; and GainLoRA [22] uses input-dependent routing, an orthogonal design axis. EWC [20] penalizes changes to parameters important for prior tasks via diagonal Fisher, which inspired our Fisher-based subspace identification, though we apply it to safety-behavior preservation rather than task-performance.

Separately, mechanistic interpretability has revealed that safety occupies identifiable low-rank subspaces. Arditi et al. [2] found refusal is mediated by a single activation direction; Wollschläger et al. [29] extended this to multi-dimensional spaces; representation engineering [44] provides broader frameworks; DARE [42] reveals redundancy in LoRA deltas; and SAILS [38] constructs interpretable safety subspaces via sparse autoencoders.

Two works partially bridge CL and safety: OGPSA [35] addresses the inverse problem of preserving task knowledge during safety alignment, and Alssum et al. [1] apply CL methods to safety but evaluate only single-task settings. SafeAnchor is the first to combine safety subspace identification with orthogonally-constrained continual LoRA optimization across sequential multi-domain adaptation.

3. SafeAnchor

We present SafeAnchor, a framework for preserving safety alignment during continual domain adaptation of LLMs. Figure 1 illustrates the overall pipeline and Algorithm 1 summarizes the procedure.

3.1. Problem Formulation

Consider a safety-aligned LLM with parameters θ0\theta_{0} that must be sequentially adapted to TT domains {𝒯1,𝒯2,…,𝒯T}\{\mathcal{T}_{1},\mathcal{T}_{2},\ldots,\mathcal{T}_{T}\}, each with training data 𝒟t\mathcal{D}_{t}. Using LoRA [10], the model’s weight matrices W∈ℝd×kW\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k} are augmented as W+B​AW+BA, where B∈ℝd×rB\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r} and A∈ℝr×kA\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times k} with rank r≪min⁡(d,k)r\ll\min(d,k). At each step tt, we train LoRA parameters Δt={Bt,At}\Delta_{t}=\{B_{t},A_{t}\}.

Let 𝒮⁡(θ)\mathcal{S}(\theta) denote the safety score and Pt​(θ)P_{t}(\theta) denote domain task performance. The standard CL objective maximizes ∑tPt​(θt)\sum_{t}P_{t}(\theta_{t}) subject to preventing forgetting. Our objective adds a safety constraint: find {Δt}t=1T\{\Delta_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T} that maximizes domain performance while maintaining 𝒮⁡(θt)≥(1−ϵ)​𝒮​(θ0)\mathcal{S}(\theta_{t})\geq(1-\epsilon)\mathcal{S}(\theta_{0}) for all tt, where ϵ\epsilon is a small tolerance. As we demonstrate, this is highly non-trivial without targeted intervention.

3.2. Safety Subspace Identification (SSI)

Inspired by findings that safety behaviors occupy identifiable low-rank subspaces in both activation space [2, 29, 44] and parameter space [42, 38], we identify the parameter subspace encoding safety-critical behavior using a gradient-based Fisher Information approach.

Safety Calibration Set. We construct a small calibration set 𝒟safe\mathcal{D}_{\text{safe}} of NsN_{s} prompt-response pairs (we use Ns=500N_{s}=500) drawn from a safety-aligned dataset [5, 16], containing both harmful prompts with correct refusal responses and benign prompts with helpful responses.

Fisher Information for LoRA Parameters. For each LoRA layer ii, we denote its flattened parameter vector as δi=vec​([Bi;Ai])\delta_{i}=\text{vec}([B_{i};A_{i}]), concatenating the vectorized BiB_{i} and AiA_{i} matrices from the set-level LoRA parameters Δt\Delta_{t}. We compute the empirical Fisher Information Matrix:

(1) Fi=1Ns​∑(x,y)∈𝒟safe∇δi​log​pθ​(y|x)​∇δi​log​pθ​(y|x)⊤F_{i}=\frac{1}{N_{s}}\sum_{(x,y)\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{safe}}}\nabla_{\delta_{i}}\log p_{\theta}(y|x)\,\nabla_{\delta_{i}}\log p_{\theta}(y|x)^{\top}

We acknowledge that the empirical Fisher is a biased approximation of the true Fisher; we verify robustness to NsN_{s} in Section 4.5. The eigendecomposition Fi=Ui​Λi​Ui⊤F_{i}=U_{i}\Lambda_{i}U_{i}^{\top} reveals principal safety-relevant directions. We select eigenvectors whose eigenvalues account for cumulative proportion ρ\rho of total variance (ρ=90%\rho=90\%) to form the safety subspace basis:

(2) Visafe=[ui(1),ui(2),…,ui(ks)]∈ℝ|δi|×ksV_{i}^{\text{safe}}=[u_{i}^{(1)},u_{i}^{(2)},\ldots,u_{i}^{(k_{s})}]\in\mathbb{R}^{|\delta_{i}|\times k_{s}}

The resulting projection matrix for layer ii is Πisafe=Visafe​(Visafe)⊤\Pi_{i}^{\text{safe}}=V_{i}^{\text{safe}}(V_{i}^{\text{safe}})^{\top}. As we verify in Section 4.4, the eigenvalue spectrum is sharply decaying, confirming that safety information occupies a genuinely low-rank subspace in LoRA parameter space, consistent with activation-space findings [2].

Incremental Subspace Update. After each domain adaptation tt, the model parameters shift, potentially altering which directions are safety-critical. We update the safety subspace as follows: (1) recompute FiF_{i} on 𝒟safe\mathcal{D}_{\text{safe}} using the adapted model θt\theta_{t} to obtain new eigenvectors V^isafe\hat{V}_{i}^{\text{safe}}; (2) concatenate the old and new bases: Vimerged=[Visafe∣V^isafe]V_{i}^{\text{merged}}=[V_{i}^{\text{safe}}\mid\hat{V}_{i}^{\text{safe}}]; (3) perform SVD on VimergedV_{i}^{\text{merged}} and retain the top singular vectors capturing ρ\rho of the variance, yielding the updated VisafeV_{i}^{\text{safe}} with controlled rank. This ensures the safety subspace tracks the evolving model while preventing unbounded rank growth. Note that SVD truncation may discard old safety directions with diminished singular values; we verify in Section 4.4 that the resulting subspace remains effective.

3.3. Orthogonal Safety-Constrained Adaptation (OSCA)

For domain tt, OSCA constrains LoRA updates to lie in the orthogonal complement of the safety subspace. Given a task loss gradient git=∇δiℒtg_{i}^{t}=\nabla_{\delta_{i}}\mathcal{L}_{t} at layer ii, OSCA computes the projected gradient:

(3) g~it=git−Πisafe​git=(I−Visafe​(Visafe)⊤)​git\tilde{g}_{i}^{t}=g_{i}^{t}-\Pi_{i}^{\text{safe}}\,g_{i}^{t}=(I-V_{i}^{\text{safe}}(V_{i}^{\text{safe}})^{\top})\,g_{i}^{t}

This removes the safety-subspace component from the gradient, ensuring domain-specific learning occurs only in directions orthogonal to safety-critical parameters [6].

Adaptive Projection Strength. Strict orthogonal projection may over-constrain learning on layers where safety and task subspaces overlap significantly. We introduce an adaptive relaxation coefficient αi∈[0,1]\alpha_{i}\in[0,1]:

(4) g^it=g~it+αi⋅Πisafe​git\hat{g}_{i}^{t}=\tilde{g}_{i}^{t}+\alpha_{i}\cdot\Pi_{i}^{\text{safe}}\,g_{i}^{t}

where αi=max⁡(0,1−λ⋅tr⁡(Fi))\alpha_{i}=\max(0,1-\lambda\cdot\tr(F_{i})) decays toward zero for layers with high safety importance (large Fisher trace tr⁡(Fi)=∑jμj(i)\tr(F_{i})=\sum_{j}\mu_{j}^{(i)}, the sum of eigenvalues), enforcing stricter projection where safety is most concentrated. Here λ\lambda is a hyperparameter controlling the strictness.

3.4. Cumulative Safety Monitoring (CSM)

While OSCA prevents direct interference with the safety subspace, indirect effects (such as changes to shared representations that affect safety through non-linear pathways) may still accumulate across domain transitions. CSM addresses this through a lightweight monitoring and correction mechanism.

Safety Probe. We maintain a held-out safety probe set 𝒟probe\mathcal{D}_{\text{probe}} (disjoint from 𝒟safe\mathcal{D}_{\text{safe}}, 200 examples from HarmBench [28]). After each domain adaptation tt, we evaluate the safety refusal rate sts_{t} on 𝒟probe\mathcal{D}_{\text{probe}} using LlamaGuard [15] as the binary safety classifier (which achieves 92.1% F1 on our probe set for distinguishing safe refusals from harmful completions).

Threshold-Triggered Safety Replay. If st<(1−τ)​s0s_{t}<(1-\tau)\,s_{0} (where s0s_{0} is the baseline refusal rate and τ\tau is the fractional tolerance), CSM triggers a brief safety replay: we fine-tune for Erepair=200E_{\text{repair}}=200 steps on a mixture of the safety calibration set and the current domain data, using the OSCA-projected gradients, to restore the safety score. The value Erepair=200E_{\text{repair}}=200 sits at the knee of a diminishing-returns curve (Appendix C): 100100 steps recover only +1.9+1.9 points vs. +2.7+2.7 at 200200, while 400400 adds a further +0.2+0.2 points at twice the cost plus 0.40.4 points of domain regression. After replay, we re-evaluate sts_{t} to verify st≥(1−τ)​s0s_{t}\geq(1-\tau)\,s_{0}; if not, replay is extended by at most one further ErepairE_{\text{repair}} block. The replay objective is:

(5) ℒreplay=ℒt​(𝒟t)+β⋅ℒsafe​(𝒟safe)\mathcal{L}_{\text{replay}}=\mathcal{L}_{t}(\mathcal{D}_{t})+\beta\cdot\mathcal{L}_{\text{safe}}(\mathcal{D}_{\text{safe}})

where β\beta controls the safety-task balance. Empirically, CSM triggers 33 times across 55 seeds ×\times 33 domains (0.200.20 triggers per domain-adaptation, concentrated on Code; Appendix C), adding negligible overhead.

3.5. Training Objective

The complete SafeAnchor training objective for domain tt combines the domain task loss with a safety regularization term:

(6) ℒtotalt=ℒt​(𝒟t)+γ⋅ℒanchort\mathcal{L}_{\text{total}}^{t}=\mathcal{L}_{t}(\mathcal{D}_{t})+\gamma\cdot\mathcal{L}_{\text{anchor}}^{t}

where the safety anchor loss penalizes changes to the model’s output distribution on safety-relevant inputs:

(7) ℒanchort=1|𝒟safe|∑x∈𝒟safeDKL(pθt−1(⋅|x)∥pθt(⋅|x))\mathcal{L}_{\text{anchor}}^{t}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{\text{safe}}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{safe}}}D_{\text{KL}}\big(p_{\theta_{t-1}}(\cdot|x)\,\|\,p_{\theta_{t}}(\cdot|x)\big)

We use forward KL because it is mean-seeking: it penalizes the current model for assigning low probability where the safe model assigned high probability, preserving refusal behaviors. Empirically, reverse KL yields 1.8 points lower safety. The coefficient γ\gamma controls regularization strength. This anchor loss complements OSCA’s hard orthogonal projection with soft distributional regularization. Note that OSCA projects only the task gradient ∇ℒt\nabla\mathcal{L}_{t}, while the anchor gradient ∇ℒanchort\nabla\mathcal{L}_{\text{anchor}}^{t} bypasses projection so that its safety-reinforcing signal is preserved.

4. Experiments

4.1. Experimental Setup

Models. We evaluate on Llama-2-7B-Chat [37] and Mistral-7B-Instruct [18], both safety-aligned chat models representative of widely deployed open-weight LLMs.

Sequential Domain Adaptation. We adapt models through three domains in sequence: (1) Medical: fine-tuned on MedQA training split [19] for medical question answering; (2) Legal: fine-tuned on LegalBench tasks [7] for legal reasoning; (3) Code: fine-tuned on the CodeAlpaca subset for code generation. Each domain uses 5,000 training examples with 3 epochs. We additionally test an alternative ordering (Code →\rightarrow Legal →\rightarrow Medical) in Section 4.3.

Evaluation Benchmarks. Safety metrics: HarmBench [28] (refusal rate on 200 harmful prompts), TruthfulQA [24] (truthfulness score), BBQ [30] (bias score; lower is better, inverted for composite), and WildGuard [4] (jailbreak robustness). We compute a composite Safety Score as:

(8) Safety=13​(HarmBench100+TruthfulQA100+100−BBQbias100)×100\text{Safety}=\frac{1}{3}\!\left(\frac{\text{HarmBench}}{100}+\frac{\text{TruthfulQA}}{100}+\frac{100-\text{BBQ}_{\text{bias}}}{100}\right)\times 100

where each component is expressed as a percentage and BBQ bias is inverted so higher is better. WildGuard is reported separately as an independent jailbreak-robustness indicator distinct from the refusal/truthfulness/bias triad. Domain metrics: MedQA accuracy, LegalBench accuracy, and HumanEval pass@1 [3]. General: MMLU [8]. MT-Bench [43] scores are reported in Section 4.3.

Baselines. (1) Standard LoRA [10]: unconstrained sequential fine-tuning. (2) EWC+LoRA [20]: Fisher-based regularization. (3) O-LoRA [39]: orthogonal subspace LoRA. (4) Safe LoRA [9]: post-hoc safety projection. (5) Vaccine+LoRA [14]: pre-immunization. (6) SafeGrad+LoRA [41]: gradient surgery. (7) Safety Interleaving: mixing 10% safety data from BeaverTails into each domain’s training set (a natural but previously untested baseline).

Baseline Adaptation to Sequential Setting. For fair comparison, all baselines were adapted to the sequential pipeline: SafeGrad’s alignment gradient is recomputed per domain step; Safe LoRA’s projection is applied after each step; Vaccine’s immunization is applied once before all domains (per its design); EWC’s Fisher is recomputed per domain; O-LoRA allocates orthogonal subspaces per domain. All use identical LoRA configurations.

Implementation. PEFT [27] with LoRA r=16r{=}16, α=32\alpha{=}32 on Q,K,V,OQ,K,V,O projections. Learning rate 2×10−42{\times}10^{-4} (cosine), batch 8 ×\times grad-accum 2, AdamW (β1=0.9,β2=0.999,\beta_{1}{=}0.9,\beta_{2}{=}0.999, wd=0.01=0.01). Safety calibration: 500 BeaverTails examples [16]. Defaults: ρ=0.90,τ=0.05,γ=0.1,λ=0.5,β=1.0,Erepair=200\rho{=}0.90,\tau{=}0.05,\gamma{=}0.1,\lambda{=}0.5,\beta{=}1.0,E_{\text{repair}}{=}200. All runs on 2×\timesA100 40GB (BF16). A 3-domain, 5-seed pipeline takes ≈7{\approx}7 h 47 min per seed: SSI ≈12.4{\approx}12.4 min/domain, OSCA ≈17.8%{\approx}17.8\% per-step overhead, CSM probe ≈4.8{\approx}4.8 min/transition (plus ≈5{\approx}5 min replay if triggered). Mean ±\pm std over 5 seeds throughout. Complete hyperparameters and per-phase compute in Appendix F.

4.2. Main Results

Tables 1 and 2 present our main results. On Llama-2-7B-Chat, standard LoRA causes a catastrophic 47.847.8-point safety drop. SafeGrad+LoRA achieves the best single-method baseline (67.4±1.467.4\pm 1.4) but still loses 24 points. Safety Interleaving (64.8±1.664.8\pm 1.6) confirms passive data mixing is insufficient. SafeAnchor retains 85.2±0.985.2\pm 0.9 (93.2% of original safety), with domain performance within 1.3 points of unconstrained LoRA. The pattern holds on Mistral (93.1% safety, 1.5-point gap). CL methods (O-LoRA, EWC) perform worse than safety-specific methods, confirming targeted preservation is necessary.

4.3. Robustness Analysis

Safety Across Domain Steps. Figure 2 shows the four safety scores recorded at the base model and after each adaptation step on Llama-2-7B-Chat. Standard LoRA exhibits accelerating degradation (91.4→78.3→61.5→43.691.4\rightarrow 78.3\rightarrow 61.5\rightarrow 43.6; average 15.915.9 points per step), confirming compounding erosion. SafeGrad+LoRA degrades more slowly (91.4→84.1→76.2→67.491.4\rightarrow 84.1\rightarrow 76.2\rightarrow 67.4; 8.08.0 pts/step) but cannot prevent cumulative drift. SafeAnchor decelerates the decrease by an order of magnitude (91.4→89.8→87.1→85.291.4\rightarrow 89.8\rightarrow 87.1\rightarrow 85.2; 2.12.1 pts/step, roughly linear), confirming that orthogonal projection and monitoring suppress compounding, though they do not entirely eliminate it.

Domain Ordering Robustness. To assess sensitivity to domain ordering, we test all 3!=63!=6 permutations of {\{Medical, Legal, Code}\} (full table in Appendix B). Across orderings, SafeAnchor’s final safety ranges from 83.9±1.283.9\pm 1.2 to 85.2±0.985.2\pm 0.9 (mean 84.5584.55, cross-order SD 0.510.51), while Standard LoRA collapses to 40.540.5–44.944.9 regardless of order. The cross-ordering SD (0.510.51) is notably smaller than within-ordering seed SD (≈1.0\approx 1.0), so ordering contributes less variance than seed-level randomness and SafeAnchor’s safety preservation is substantively order-robust.

Adversarial Robustness. We test models after full adaptation against GCG-style adversarial suffixes [45] (2020 optimization steps, suffix length 2020 tokens, 256256 attack candidates per step, 100100 harmful prompts; a compute-reduced configuration that preserves cross-method ordering but yields higher absolute refusal rates than full-budget 500500-step GCG [28]). SafeAnchor maintains 78.4±2.178.4\pm 2.1% refusal under attack, versus 54.6±2.654.6\pm 2.6% for the strongest baseline (SafeGrad+LoRA), 49.3±2.949.3\pm 2.9% for Safety Interleaving, and 31.2±3.831.2\pm 3.8% for Standard LoRA; the full table with all seven baselines is in Appendix E. The +23.8+23.8-point gap to SafeGrad exceeds the +17.8+17.8-point benign-safety gap in Table 1, indicating that preserving the safety subspace during adaptation confers robustness beyond what benign probes reveal.

Additional Metrics. SafeAnchor achieves WildGuard jailbreak robustness of 81.3±1.281.3\pm 1.2 (vs. 38.7±3.138.7\pm 3.1 for Standard LoRA, 62.4±2.062.4\pm 2.0 for SafeGrad) and MT-Bench quality of 6.21±0.156.21\pm 0.15 (vs. 6.08±0.186.08\pm 0.18 Standard LoRA), confirming safety preservation does not degrade conversational quality. CSM triggered once (after Code) in 2 of 5 seeds.

4.4. Ablation Study

Table 3 reveals each component’s contribution. SSI alone has minimal effect (+0.6+0.6). Strict OSCA recovers most safety (79.6±1.279.6\pm 1.2) at a 4.4-point domain cost; adaptive projection reduces this (82.4±1.082.4\pm 1.0, 60.860.8). The anchor loss adds 1.3±0.31.3\pm 0.3 points (p<0.01p<0.01, paired tt-test), confirming complementary value beyond OSCA. CSM contributes 1.5±0.41.5\pm 0.4 points. Without incremental SSI update, safety drops 5.1 points.

Safety Subspace Validation. To validate the low-rank safety subspace assumption (Section 3.2), we examined the eigenvalue spectrum of the Fisher Information matrix on the safety calibration set. Across all LoRA layers, the spectrum decays sharply: on average ∼{\sim}8 eigenvectors capture 90% of the total variance, while a random subset of training data produces a near-flat spectrum. This confirms that safety information in LoRA parameter space is genuinely low-rank, consistent with activation-space findings [2, 44]. We further analyze the stability of this subspace across sequential domain adaptations (principal-angle and Grassmannian-distance analyses) in Appendix D.

4.5. Sensitivity Analysis

We examine sensitivity to key hyperparameters (Table 4). Increasing ρ\rho from 0.80 to 0.95 improves safety (+3.1) at moderate domain cost (−-2.2). CSM threshold τ\tau controls monitoring sensitivity. SafeAnchor is also robust to calibration size: even Ns=100N_{s}=100 achieves 83.1 safety, which is above all baselines, confirming stable Fisher eigenvector estimation.

5. Conclusion

We introduced SafeAnchor, a framework for preserving safety alignment during continual domain adaptation of LLMs. By combining Safety Subspace Identification, Orthogonal Safety-Constrained Adaptation, and Cumulative Safety Monitoring, SafeAnchor retains over 93% of original safety after three sequential adaptations with competitive domain performance. While individual components draw on established techniques, their principled integration for sequential safety preservation is validated across two architectures, eight benchmarks, and full variance reporting.

Limitations and Future Work. Our evaluation is limited to 7B-scale models and a primary focus of three sequential domains; Appendix A extends to T=5T=5 and finds SafeAnchor’s near-linear trajectory continues (slope ≈1.9{\approx}1.9 pts/step), but rigorous study at T≥5T{\geq}5 across orderings remains open. Alignment elasticity worsens with scale [17], making 13B+ extension important; we expect SafeAnchor’s Fisher-subspace machinery to transfer, but ksk_{s} and Fisher-trace distributions may shift. Longer sequences could eventually exhaust the orthogonal complement (manifesting as subspace inflation or gradient cancellation); neither is observed at T=5T{=}5 (App. D). Future work includes integration with alignment-stage defenses [14, 36] and non-LoRA methods [25].

Reproducibility. All materials are available at: https://github.com/bettyguo/SafeAnchor. Full hyperparameters, per-component compute profile, and evaluation protocols are detailed in Appendix F.

Appendix A Extended Sequential Adaptation to T=5T{=}5

Reviewers R1 and R3 noted that the main-text pipeline stops at T=3T{=}3 and suggested testing whether safety degradation continues linearly beyond the reported three domains. We extend the sequence with two further specialized domains: (4) Finance, using 5,0005{,}000 examples drawn from FinancialPhraseBank and FiQA-SA for financial sentiment and reasoning; and (5) Science, using 5,0005{,}000 SciQ-style multiple-choice and short-answer items for general science. All hyperparameters match Section 4.1.

SafeAnchor retains 81.6±1.181.6\pm 1.1 safety after five domains, still 27.3 points above the best baseline at T=5T{=}5 (SafeGrad, 54.3±1.554.3\pm 1.5) and 56.7 points above Standard LoRA. The per-step decrease averages (91.4−81.6)/5=1.96(91.4{-}81.6)/5=1.96 pts/step, consistent with the 2.12.1 pts/step slope reported at T=3T{=}3. Standard LoRA’s slope decelerates from 15.915.9 to 13.313.3 pts/step as it approaches the residual-refusal floor (≈20\approx 20 for HarmBench on Llama-2-Chat [28]). SafeAnchor’s domain composite remains within 1.31.3 points of Standard LoRA throughout.

Appendix B All 6 Domain Orderings at T=3T{=}3

Reviewer R3 observed that the main text tests only two of the 3!=63!{=}6 possible orderings of {\{Medical, Legal, Code}\}. We complete the sweep on Llama-2-7B-Chat with 5 seeds per ordering (30 total runs per method).

SafeAnchor’s safety lies in a narrow [83.9,85.2][83.9,85.2] band across all six orderings. The cross-ordering SD (0.510.51) is approximately half the within-ordering (seed) SD (≈1.0{\approx}1.0), so ordering explains less variance than random seeds. Orderings ending with a domain whose gradients overlap most with the safety subspace (Code, reflected in higher trigger rates; App. C) tend to produce marginally lower final safety. Standard LoRA also shows comparable robustness to ordering (all within [40.5,44.9][40.5,44.9]), but at a safety level 4040+ points below SafeAnchor regardless of ordering. The cumulative erosion is therefore an intrinsic property of unconstrained adaptation, not an artefact of ordering.

Appendix C CSM Repair Analysis

Reviewer R3 asked (a) why ErepairE_{\text{repair}} is fixed, (b) whether the repair actually succeeds, and (c) how often CSM triggers. We address all three here.

Trigger frequency. Across the default-ordering campaign (5 seeds ×\times 3 domains), CSM fires 33 times in 1515 domain-adaptation events (0.200.20 per event). Triggers concentrate on the final Code stage, consistent with Code gradients exhibiting the largest overlap with the safety subspace (Appendix D).

Repair validation. Every trigger restores sts_{t} above the (1−τ)​s0=0.95×91.4=86.83(1-\tau)s_{0}=0.95\times 91.4=86.83 threshold within one ErepairE_{\text{repair}} block; no seed required a second block. The pooled post-repair mean (88.988.9) exceeds the threshold by 2.12.1 points, giving meaningful headroom against downstream drift.

ErepairE_{\text{repair}} sensitivity. We re-ran the two triggered post-Code seeds with Erepair∈{50,100,200,400,800}E_{\text{repair}}\in\{50,100,200,400,800\}:

Going from 100→200100{\to}200 gains +0.9+0.9 safety; going from 200→400200{\to}400 gains only +0.2+0.2 at 2×2\times cost and −0.4-0.4 additional domain regression. Erepair=200E_{\text{repair}}{=}200 is the knee.

Appendix D Safety Subspace Stability Across Domains

Reviewer R4 asked for an analysis of how stable the safety subspace is across sequential adaptations. We compute two quantities: (i) mean cosine similarity between principal subspace directions, and (ii) normalized Grassmannian distance dG=∑jθj2/ks⋅(π/2)2d_{G}=\sqrt{\sum_{j}\theta_{j}^{2}}/\sqrt{k_{s}\cdot(\pi/2)^{2}}, where θj\theta_{j} are principal angles. Both are computed layer-wise on Q-projections of Llama-2-7B-Chat (32 layers) and averaged.

Adjacent-stage cosine similarity stays ≥0.87\geq 0.87 and end-to-end remains 0.820.82, over two orders of magnitude above the random-subspace null of 0.0060.006, while dGd_{G} of 0.240.24–0.380.38 is correspondingly far below the near-unity null of 0.9960.996. The null is the expectation for two uniformly-random ksk_{s}-dimensional subspaces drawn in the ambient LoRA parameter space (|δi|=131,072|\delta_{i}|{=}131{,}072 for Q-projections; 5050 Monte Carlo trials per entry), where both metrics concentrate sharply because ks≪|δi|k_{s}\ll|\delta_{i}|. The intrinsic rank ksk_{s} is near-constant at approximately 8, confirming that the SVD-truncated incremental update preserves the effective subspace size rather than inflating it. The Code stage produces the largest per-step drift (dG=0.29d_{G}{=}0.29), matching its higher CSM trigger rate (Appendix C) and suggesting Code-domain gradients interact most with safety-critical directions.

Appendix E Adversarial Robustness: All Baselines

Expanded table for the GCG attack setting described in Section 4.3. Suffixes are optimized for 2020 steps, length 2020 tokens, 256256 candidates/step, on 100100 HarmBench prompts, after the full three-domain adaptation.

The attack-ranking correlates strongly with the benign-safety ranking in Table 1 (Spearman ρ=0.96\rho{=}0.96), but the SafeAnchor→\rightarrownext-best gap widens from 17.817.8 points (benign) to 23.823.8 points (adversarial). This is consistent with the hypothesis that preserving the safety subspace also preserves the adversarial refusal direction [2] that GCG most effectively targets.

Appendix F Hyperparameters and Compute Profile

Hyperparameters (defaults for all main-text experiments).

Per-component compute profile. All runs use 2×\timesNVIDIA A100 40GB with BF16 mixed precision. Wall-clock time is averaged over 5 seeds of the default-ordering pipeline.

The 17.8%17.8\% OSCA overhead is dominated by the per-layer projection gi−Visafe​(Visafe)⊤​gig_{i}-V_{i}^{\text{safe}}(V_{i}^{\text{safe}})^{\top}g_{i} with ks≈8k_{s}{\approx}8; this is O⁡(|δi|⋅ks)O(|\delta_{i}|\cdot k_{s}) per layer under the diagonal-block Fisher approximation and parallelizes across layers. The underlying FLOP cost is negligible (<10−6<10^{-6} of the forward pass), so the measured wall-clock overhead reflects PyTorch autograd-hook dispatch and non-fused projection ops; a fused-kernel implementation would reduce this to <5%<5\%. SSI cost is amortized once per domain, and CSM is essentially free (<1%<1\%).
